description: Developing an innovative tool to explore SPHEREx data.
summary:
Skytrace is a free, public, and open-source web application that implements NASA’s SPHEREx mission data sets into an interactive sky visualisation web tool. Through entering coordinates, searching by object name, or clicking on the interactive sky map, users can identify NASA’s IRSA archive in real time, retrieve multi-epoch SPHEREx imaging, and explore changes over time through observations visit by visit. This temporal stacking and blinking mechanism allows proper motion, transient phenomena, and luminosity variations to be displayed.
Skytrace features pre-configured test targets alongside advanced analysis tools: per-detector pixel stacks, on-the-fly spectral energy distributions (SEDs) spanning 0.75-5 µm for every observation, image subtraction capabilities, field-of-view adjustments, Gaia and WISE catalog overlays, SPHEREx data quality flags, allows for sharing URLs, and Aladin Lite integration.

The automated validation is highly reliable, as in injection tests with 288 simulated sources, the automated moving-object detection algorithm successfully isolated candidates while not reporting false positives on stationary sources. Skytrace makes the overall process more efficient, thus creating significant impact through education and accelerating innovation so students, teachers, citizen scientists, and astronomers can easily explore NASA data in an interactive, visualised web tool.
details:
What it does & how it works
Skytrace is an interactive, open-source web application designed to allow access to NASA’s SPHEREx mission data to the public. The tool allows users to enter coordinates, search by object name, or click anywhere on an interactive sky map to retrieve NASA’s IRSA archive in real time.

When a target is selected, Skytrace fetches sequential observations, letting users explore changes over time through a visit-by-visit interface which was inspired by historical astronomical discovery techniques (e.g, the blink method used to find Pluto). Key exploration modes are:

  • Step through individual six-monthly survey visits or subtract reference frames to instantly highlight moving or variable objects.
  • Slide images along a trial motion vector to stack frames and enhance faint, fast-moving objects.
  • Traverse all 102 individual infrared spectral channels 0.75-5 µm to create an on-the-fly "spectrum movie".

Benefits, impact, & creativity

  • While discovering nearby brown dwarfs and transient celestial bodies traditionally required professional pipelines or time consuming manual comparisons, Skytrace makes this analysis accessible to students, educators, citizen scientists, and professional astronomers alike.
  • To prevent false positives caused by changing filter passbands, Skytrace implements same-band blinking, alongside multi-survey catalog overlays (Gaia DR3, CatWISE, 2MASS, and DSS2), SPHEREx data quality contamination flags, and interactive molecular band markers (H2O, CH4, CO2, CO).
  • By supporting persistent shareable URLs, classroom embeds, and automated candidate export options (PDF), Skytrace allows users to share discoveries, thus encouraging engagement with NASA's massive all-sky survey data.

Tools, Languages, Hardware, & Software

  • Developed in Python using FastAPI, Astropy, astroquery, PyVO, photutils, and SciPy to query NASA IRSA’s SIA service at runtime, execute efficient byte-range reads from IRSA’s public AWS open data bucket, remove zodiacal light, and measure targets on original detector pixels matching official IRSA SPHEREx Source Discovery Tool tutorials.
  • It is built with JavaScript, Bootstrap 5, Plotly.js, Aladin Lite, and jsPDF, allowing responsive, client-side data rendering and live analysis.
  • The web tool is hosted on Google Cloud Run and published as open-source software under the Apache-2.0 license on GitHub (prs127/skytrace).

Team Considerations & Validation

  • Preloads all major challenge benchmarks (including Barnard’s Star, Epsilon Indi B, WISE 0855, RW Aurigae, and R Draconis) for evaluation.
  • Photometry matches tutorial pipelines to within 2 parts per million, and astrometric mover tracking successfully recovers benchmarks like WISE 0855 and Epsilon Indi B, while tests involving 288 synthetic sources yield zero false positives on stationary background objects.
  • It is designed with a visual layout, a step-by-step onboarding guide ("New Here?"), panel-level help buttons, and dynamic field-of-view adjustments to balance data transfer speeds with wide-field tracking capabilities.
